clue_1: In 2012 he was inducted into rugby league's most exclusive club, becoming the first player from the modern era to be granted the sport's highest individual honour, and only the eighth man ever to receive it
clue_2: His career was cut short in 2007 by chronic neck and spinal problems that had been quietly grinding him down for years, and he later admitted he had taken painkillers on the field during the back half of his career simply to keep playing
clue_3: He is the only player ever to have won the Dally M Medal three times, claiming it in 1998, 1999 and 2002, and twice was awarded the Golden Boot as the best player in the world
clue_4: He spent his entire 14-season career at the Newcastle Knights, with whom he won grand finals in 1997 and 2001 alongside his older brother Matthew
clue_5: Recalled to the New South Wales Origin side in 2005 with his career almost over, he produced one of the great cameos in series history, the late field goal he kicked in Game Three turning the contest
clue_6: Newcastle Knights halfback nicknamed 'Joey' (1993-2007), three-time Dally M Medallist, two-time premiership winner and the eighth Immortal of rugby league
facts: In a 2007 television interview he admitted to taking the drug ecstasy regularly throughout much of his playing career, a confession that cost him commentary and media work for several years before he was eventually rehabilitated by Channel Nine.
He has spoken openly about a long battle with bipolar disorder, becoming one of Australian sport's most prominent advocates for mental-health awareness.
His grandfather gave him the nickname 'Joey' as a young child, after Joe Kangaroo from a popular Australian cartoon, and it stuck for life.

clue_1: Late in 2022 he voluntarily admitted himself to a Sydney rehabilitation clinic to deal with a gambling problem that had begun to consume his finances, putting an end-of-year Australian tour and the start of pre-season on hold
clue_2: Months later, returning from rehab, the same player turned down what was widely reported as the richest contract ever offered to an NRL footballer, choosing to stay loyal to the southern club that had developed him since 2014
clue_3: He has been named Dally M Five-Eighth of the Year three times across his career and was awarded the Wally Lewis Medal as player of the 2022 State of Origin series
clue_4: He was the dominant ball-running playmaker when his club won the 2020 NRL grand final, defeating Penrith 26-20
clue_5: Now the senior playmaker of the Queensland State of Origin side, he has inherited the role left vacant by the retirements of Cameron Smith, Cooper Cronk and Johnathan Thurston
clue_6: Melbourne Storm five-eighth from Rockhampton (2014-present), 2020 NRL premiership winner, three-time Dally M five-eighth of the year and Wally Lewis Medallist for Queensland
facts: Before turning professional he worked summer holidays on a council crew laying bitumen on the roads of central Queensland, a job he has often credited with teaching him not to take a football career for granted.
He was the first man ever to be named the Wally Lewis Medallist as the player of an Origin series after his side had trailed 0-1 in the contest.
His on-field nickname 'The Munster' is a play on the cartoon character, and the Storm marketing department once licensed an officially-branded green-and-purple mascot version of him.

clue_1: He toured England, France or Papua New Guinea with the Australian national team on four separate occasions between 1982 and 1994, a feat no other rugby league player has ever achieved and one that almost certainly never will be
clue_2: At 192 centimetres and 105 kilograms he was an immense, freakishly strong centre who ran through tacklers like few backs ever had, but before his international career took off he was a young Queensland police constable, fitting weekend football around shifts in uniform
clue_3: He broke his arm four times across the 1986 and 1987 seasons after moving south to join an expansion club, and briefly considered retirement before recovering to become his side's most-celebrated player
clue_4: He captained that southern expansion club to grand-final victories in 1989, 1990 and 1994, the only premierships the team won in his playing era
clue_5: Named an Australian Immortal in 2018, he has coached the Australian Kangaroos national side since 2016, including their 2017 Rugby League World Cup triumph
clue_6: Canberra Raiders centre (1986-1994), three-time premiership-winning captain, four-time Kangaroo tourist, an Immortal of the game and long-serving coach of the Kangaroos
facts: He played most of his Brisbane junior football for the Souths Logan club, and turned out for St Helens in the English league during the 1984-85 northern winter, scoring a hat-trick in his very first appearance for the club.
After retirement he ran for the Queensland state seat of Bundamba as a Labor candidate in 2001, but withdrew his candidacy mid-campaign citing the stress of public political life.
He was made a Member of the Order of Australia in 1991 for his services to rugby league, and was given the keys to the city of Canberra in 1994.

clue_1: For more than a decade he was the most under-appreciated craftsman in the Australian game, a quiet, country-bred playmaker who set up tries for everyone around him through a sidestep so prized that opposition coaches devoted whole game-plans simply to denying him the ball
clue_2: He made his first-grade debut for the Norths Devils in the Brisbane competition in 1985, before being lured south by a Sydney club where he spent the next 13 seasons as the team's creative heart
clue_3: He played in two grand-final winning sides nearly a decade apart, in 1987 and 1996, and was awarded the Clive Churchill Medal as the best player on the field in the second of those deciders
clue_4: His Sydney club was the Manly-Warringah Sea Eagles, for whom he played 332 first-grade games and was named in the official Team of the Century in 2008
clue_5: He represented New South Wales 18 times and Australia on four occasions, including the 1992 Rugby League World Cup final at Wembley Stadium, which Australia won 10-6 over Great Britain
clue_6: Manly Sea Eagles five-eighth nicknamed 'Cliffy' (1986-1998), a two-time premiership winner and 1996 Clive Churchill Medallist whose ball-playing artistry made him one of the most-loved Northern Beaches players of his generation
facts: He played his junior football for the Wauchope Blues on the Mid-North Coast of New South Wales, leaving school early to take up a rugby league apprenticeship in Brisbane.

His regular halves partner at Manly across multiple seasons was the future championship-winning coach Des Hasler, with whom he formed one of the most enduring playmaking combinations of the late 1980s.
After retirement he worked for some years as a development coach at the Manly Sea Eagles, mentoring young halves through the club's junior pathway.

clue_1: An Australian federal Senator who served from 2014 to 2016, one of the very few professional footballers to ever sit in the Commonwealth Parliament, he had previously anchored the front rows of three different NRL premiership-winning teams in three different cities
clue_2: At 192 centimetres and 110 kilograms he was the kind of immovable, square-shouldered front-rower for whom the nickname 'Brick With Eyes' could only ever fit, a man whose entire playing style was built around grinding the heaviest possible metres up the middle of the field
clue_3: He won grand finals with the Canberra Raiders in 1989 and 1990, with the Brisbane Broncos in 1992 and 1993, and with the Melbourne Storm in 1999, becoming one of the very few men ever to win an NRL title at three different clubs
clue_4: He was the foundation captain of the Melbourne Storm when the club joined the competition in 1998, leading the side to its first ever premiership in only its second season
clue_5: He played 19 State of Origin matches for New South Wales between 1991 and 1998, and toured with the Kangaroos in 1990 and 1994
clue_6: Front-row forward nicknamed 'Brick With Eyes' who played for the Canberra Raiders, Brisbane Broncos and Melbourne Storm between 1987 and 1999, winning premierships at all three clubs, and who later served as a federal Senator for Queensland
facts: He was elected to the Australian Senate in 2013 as a candidate for the Palmer United Party, before resigning from the party in March 2015 and serving out the rest of his term as an independent.
Before being signed by Canberra he had been working in his uncle's panel-beating shop in Queanbeyan, and had given serious consideration to leaving rugby league for a regular trade.
He runs a roadhouse and truck stop on the Bruce Highway in central Queensland, which he opened with his wife after retiring from politics.

clue_1: With his platinum-bleached hair, oversized diamond earrings and famous on-field swagger, he became one of the most heavily marketed teenagers in the history of Australian rugby league, fronting national advertising campaigns before he had played 50 first-grade games
clue_2: Born in 2002, he was signed by a Brisbane club as a 15-year-old, traded to the New Zealand Warriors at 17, then sensationally traded back to Brisbane three years later in a deal that involved more than half a dozen players changing direction
clue_3: He was named in the Dally M Team of the Year in 2023 as a 20-year-old, in his first full season since returning to his original club
clue_4: He led the Brisbane Broncos to the 2023 grand final against Penrith, an unforgettable decider in which the Broncos led by 16 points before losing 26-24 in the final minutes
clue_5: Now Queensland's first-choice State of Origin fullback, he was a central figure in the Maroons' 2024 series victory over New South Wales
clue_6: Brisbane Broncos fullback, earlier of the New Zealand Warriors, a 2023 grand-final runner-up who plays State of Origin for Queensland and represents the New Zealand Kiwis through his mother's heritage
facts: In Game 1 of the 2024 State of Origin series he was knocked out by a high shot from Roosters wing Joseph Suaalii, who became the first player sent off in an Origin match in nearly four decades.
He grew up between the Gold Coast and his mother's hometown in the Bay of Plenty in New Zealand, splitting school holidays between the two countries.
After his trade back to Brisbane he was briefly the youngest player in NRL history to be signed to a million-dollar-a-season contract, at the age of 20.

clue_1: In a State of Origin match in 2002 he carried a Blues fullback bodily over the touchline, swinging him by the scruff of the jersey like a bag of washing, in a moment that has been replayed thousands of times and that defined an era of forwards play
clue_2: Born in 1973 in north Queensland, he was a chronic non-conformist who left St George under a cloud in 1995 to sign a Super League contract with a Brisbane club, triggering a court case that kept him out of football for nearly an entire season
clue_3: He played a starring role in two premiership-winning sides in 1998 and 2000, both under coach Wayne Bennett, by which time he had completed his return to Queensland
clue_4: He went on to captain the Brisbane Broncos, Queensland and Australia, becoming one of the most marketable enforcers the game has ever produced
clue_5: A serious neck injury forced him into early retirement in 2004 at just 31 years of age, after which he reinvented himself as one of the most recognisable rugby league television and radio personalities in the country
clue_6: Brisbane Broncos and earlier St George Dragons backrower nicknamed 'The Raging Bull', a two-time premiership winner who captained Australia and Queensland, and now a long-time NRL television and radio commentator
facts: He is of Samoan and Italian heritage, and the unusual 'e' in his first name was a gift from his father, who borrowed the spelling from the actor Gorden Kaye of the British sitcom 'Allo 'Allo!.
The Blues fullback he memorably dragged over the sideline in 2002 was Brett Hodgson, then a small, lightly-built rookie just six games into his first-grade career, and the two men remain friends.
His coaching career has been limited to brief stints with the Indigenous All-Stars and with junior Brisbane representative sides, despite repeated approaches from NRL clubs.

clue_1: In 2015 he signed a four-year contract with the Canberra Raiders, only to refuse to honour it a fortnight later. He paid a substantial financial penalty to stay at his original Sydney club, where he played another two seasons before engineering a move to a more successful Sydney rival
clue_2: His new Sydney club promptly won back-to-back premierships, and he was the player at the centre of both wins, a balanced, scything fullback whose ability to ghost through traffic and offload in contact made him the dominant ball-running custodian of his generation
clue_3: He won the Dally M Medal in 2018 and again in 2019, and was named in the Dally M Team of the Year in nine of his first eleven seasons
clue_4: A long-time captain of New South Wales and Australia, he led the Blues to State of Origin series wins in 2019 and 2021 and the Kangaroos to a Rugby League World Cup title in 2022
clue_5: In 2024 he became just the third player in club history to register 200 NRL games for the Sydney Roosters
clue_6: Sydney Roosters fullback, earlier of the Wests Tigers, a two-time NRL premiership winner, two-time Dally M Medallist and captain of both the Blues and the Kangaroos in his prime
facts: He comes from an Italian-Australian family that has run a delicatessen in western Sydney since the 1970s, and he has spoken about his nonna's lasagne as the secret to his playing weight.
He captained the Kangaroos to the 2022 Rugby League World Cup title in England, defeating Samoa 30-10 in the final at Old Trafford in his first major tournament as captain.
His younger brother Anthony has also played professional rugby league, turning out for the Melbourne Storm and the New Zealand Warriors during the early 2020s.

clue_1: At the end of the 2021 NRL season, at the absolute peak of his powers as a former Dally M Medallist and Golden Boot winner, he walked away from rugby league entirely, switching codes to play rugby union for the Auckland Blues and the All Blacks
clue_2: He stayed away from his original code for two and a half years, played at a Rugby World Cup, and then returned to his former club and his former captaincy in 2024, in one of the most unusual career arcs of the modern era
clue_3: He had begun his NRL career at the Sydney Roosters as a teenager, and played on the wing for the side that beat the Manly Sea Eagles in the 2013 grand final
clue_4: But he is best remembered as the long-serving captain of the New Zealand Warriors, the side he joined in 2016 and led for the next six seasons
clue_5: He was named the Dally M Medallist in 2018 and the Golden Boot winner in the same year, only the second player from his club ever to be given either honour
clue_6: New Zealand Warriors fullback nicknamed 'RTS' (2016-2021 and 2024-present), a 2013 NRL premiership winner with the Sydney Roosters, 2018 Dally M Medallist and Golden Boot winner, and long-time captain of the New Zealand Kiwis
facts: He represented New Zealand in rugby union at the 2023 Rugby World Cup in France, becoming one of the very few players to play both rugby league and rugby union at international level in the modern era.
He suffered a ruptured anterior cruciate ligament in 2017 that was widely expected to end his career, before recovering to win the Dally M Medal in his very next full season.
He is a vocal Christian who has spoken about his faith as the foundation of his career, and serves as an ambassador for several youth and family charities in south Auckland.

clue_1: He arrived at the Melbourne Storm as a young development hooker in 2017 to find his path to first grade blocked by no less a figure than the most-capped player in NRL history, the man for whom the club's number-nine jersey had effectively been written
clue_2: To get him game time the club farmed him out to the Wests Tigers for the whole of 2020, where he played enough rugby league to be named the Dally M Rookie of the Year despite having not played a single first-grade match for his parent club
clue_3: He returned to Melbourne in 2021 to step directly into the retired Cameron Smith's shoes, and went on to be named Dally M Hooker of the Year in both 2022 and 2023
clue_4: He is now Queensland's first-choice State of Origin hooker, having taken the Maroons number-nine jersey once worn by his decorated club predecessor
clue_5: He was part of the Melbourne side that lost the 2024 grand final to Penrith, and in the same year signed a contract extension keeping him at the club until at least 2027
clue_6: Melbourne Storm hooker from Mackay (2020-present), 2020 Dally M Rookie of the Year and two-time Dally M Hooker of the Year, who plays State of Origin for Queensland and represents the Kangaroos
facts: He scored a famous match-winning try in his very first State of Origin appearance for Queensland, in Game Two of the 2020 series, after being elevated from the bench late in the second half.

The 2020 player swap that sent him to the Wests Tigers also involved halfback Brodie Croft moving from Melbourne to Brisbane via the Tigers, in one of the most complicated three-club deals in modern NRL history.
He grew up a passionate Sydney Roosters fan and has said he had a Brad Fittler poster on his bedroom wall as a child in central Queensland.
